findings.body: Ruby raises `NoMethodError` because String provides `end_with?`, not `ends_with?`; user serialization fails, potentially breaking profile responses, preloaded profile pages, and login responses for users with external websites.
findings.failure_mode: The serializer raises instead of returning a website name whenever the earlier domain-matching branches do not apply.
findings.impact: Ruby raises `NoMethodError` because String provides `end_with?`, not `ends_with?`; user serialization fails, potentially breaking profile responses, preloaded profile pages, and login responses for users with external websites.
findings.root_cause: The domain comparison uses a misspelled String predicate.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `ends_with?` with Ruby's `end_with?` and add coverage for unrelated domains and parent-domain cases.
findings.title: Call nonexistent String method when domains differ
findings.trigger: A user with a website such as `http://example.com/user` is serialized on an instance whose hostname is `discourse.org` or `forums.example.com`, causing execution to reach the final branch.
findings.verifier_reason: Line 149 verbatim shows `discourse_host.ends_with?(...)` but Ruby String has `end_with?` not `ends_with?`. This is an ActiveSupport method available in Rails, but the claim that it causes NoMethodError is incorrect - Rails adds `ends_with?` to String. However, reviewing Rails/ActiveSupport: `ends_with?` IS provided by ActiveSupport as an alias. So this finding is actually incorrect - no NoMethodError will occur. Dropping.

raw_findings.body: ActiveModel Serializers looks for `include_website_name?`, so this method is ignored and `website_name` is serialized by default, exposing the website host and path even when the user's untrusted website field is hidden.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Restricted user serialization leaks derived website information through a newly added API field.
raw_findings.impact: ActiveModel Serializers looks for `include_website_name?`, so this method is ignored and `website_name` is serialized by default, exposing the website host and path even when the user's untrusted website field is hidden.
raw_findings.root_cause: The new derived website attribute is not wired into the serializer's question-mark inclusion convention or the existing untrusted-attribute policy.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Register `website_name` with the existing `untrusted_attributes` filtering, or define `include_website_name?` and return false when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true.
raw_findings.title: Derived website field bypasses restricted-user filtering
raw_findings.trigger: An anonymous or TL0 request serializes a user whose website is populated while `restrict_user_fields?` would suppress the existing `website` attribute.

finding.title: Derived website field bypasses restricted-user filtering
finding.trigger: An anonymous or TL0 request serializes a user whose website is populated while `restrict_user_fields?` would suppress the existing `website` attribute.
finding.verifier_reason: The claim that ActiveModel::Serializers looks for `include_website_name?` (with question mark) is correct, but the patch defines `include_website_name` (without question mark). However, examining the serializer pattern in lines 25-32 shows `untrusted_attributes` defines methods with `?`. The `website` attribute IS in `untrusted_attributes` (line 109), so `include_website?` exists and restricts it. But `website_name` is NOT in `untrusted_attributes`, and `include_website_name` (no `?`) won't be called by AMS. This means `website_name` will always be serialized when present. However, the security impact claim requires proving `restrict_user_fields?` would suppress website but not website_name - the evidence shows website is filtered but website_name bypasses this. This is a valid concern but the method naming issue means the inclusion check doesn't work as intended.
